readerTitle: Your note app is good. Why would anyone switch?
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (노트 앱 스타트업 + 고객사인 컨설팅·디자인 에이전시 + 호텔 그룹) · 모든 인물, 회사, 상황은 설명용
insight: 포지셔닝은 제품을 바꾸는 일이 아니라 고객이 무엇과 비교하고, 무엇을 이유로 고르고, 어떤 한 단어로 기억할지를 정하는 일이다.
misconception: 좋은 제품이면 '모두를 위한 제품'이라고 넓게 말할수록 더 많은 고객이 온다. 좁게 포지셔닝하면 다른 고객을 잃는다.

sources.text: Ries, A. & Trout, J. (1981). Positioning: The Battle for Your Mind. McGraw-Hill.
Keller, K. L., Sternthal, B. & Tybout, A. (2002). Three Questions You Need to Ask About Your Brand. Harvard Business Review.
시나리오와 인물, 회사는 모두 설명용 가상 사례

factChecks.note: 시나리오 전체가 가상 사례이며 실제 통계나 기업 수치는 쓰지 않았습니다. '수백 명 가입, 대부분 이탈', '에이전시 10곳보다 많은 금액' 등은 설명용 표현입니다.
출처 서지 정보(Ries & Trout 1981 초판, Keller·Sternthal·Tybout 2002 HBR 9월호)를 게시 전에 다시 확인하세요. 카드 본문에는 출처를 직접 인용하지 않았습니다.
실제 노트 앱 브랜드명은 쓰지 않았습니다. '무료 노트 앱', '대형 노트 앱'처럼 일반 표현만 사용했는지 최종 검토 시 확인하세요.

cards.title: Your note app is good. Why would anyone switch?
body: You and a co-founder built a note-taking app. It's fast and clean, and it does one clever thing: it turns messy meeting notes into a tidy summary and action list in seconds.
Your launch page says *Notes for everyone*. Hundreds of people sign up. Most never come back. Over the next four decisions, you decide how to position it.

image.label: A lone notebook app icon lost in a crowd of similar icons
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 비슷하게 생긴 노트 앱 아이콘 수십 개가 빽빽하게 놓여 있고, 그 가운데 주인공 앱 아이콘 하나만 살짝 다른 색. 실제 앱 로고나 상표는 절대 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What should customers compare you with?
body: You look at who stays and spot a pattern: small consulting and design agencies. They use the app in client meetings, then send the summary straight to the client.
How do you describe the app now?

options.feedback: Now you're judged against free apps people already use every day. Being a bit better rarely beats free and familiar.

options.text: The meeting notebook for client-service firms
options.feedback: Agencies now compare you with what they really use for this job: scribbled notes and a recap email typed late at night. You win that comparison easily.
It sounds big, but buyers can't tell what it replaces or who it's for. A vague label makes customers do the positioning work themselves, and most won't.

cards.title: What goes first on the homepage?
body: Say you chose *the meeting notebook for client-service firms*. Now you need the one reason to pick you. Your team suggests three headlines.

options.text: Fast, beautiful and syncs on every device
options.feedback: All true, and all needed. But every rival says the same, so it gives no reason to choose you. These are entry tickets, not reasons.

options.text: Your client gets the recap before you leave the room
options.feedback: It matters to the buyer, you do it better than their current habit, and general note apps aren't built around it. That makes it a real point of difference.

options.text: Half the price of other note apps
options.feedback: Price is easy to claim and easy to match. Against free tools, you'd start a race you can't win and attract customers who leave for the next deal.

cards.title: Sales wants to show all twelve features.
body: Say you chose the recap headline. Your first sales hire says buyers ask about tags, templates, search and more. She wants one slide listing all twelve features.

options.text: Show all twelve. More features, more reasons to buy
options.feedback: Twelve claims blur into none. Buyers remember about one idea per brand, and a long list buries the one that made you different.

options.text: Lead with one word, *recap*, and cover the rest when asked
options.feedback: You build one clear memory: the recap app. The other features still help close deals, but they support the main idea instead of competing with it.

options.text: Coin a new category: *Client Intelligence Platform*
options.feedback: A new category can make you its leader, but first you must teach the market what it means. That takes time and money a small team rarely has.

cards.title: Same product, a much clearer story.
body: Say you chose *recap*. Agencies now describe you in one sentence: "It's the app that sends the client recap." They tell other agencies in those same words.

The product barely changed. What changed was **who it's for, what it replaces, and the one reason to pick it.** That is positioning: the place your product holds in a customer's mind, next to the options they already know.

image.label: Before and after: a crowded note-app shelf versus a clear spot labeled recap
image.brief: 좌우 비교 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 'Before': 'Notes for everyone' 라벨이 붙은 앱이 비슷한 앱들 사이에 묻혀 있음. 오른쪽 'After': 'Scribbled notes', 'Late-night recap email' 옆에 'Recap' 라벨이 붙은 앱이 또렷하게 서 있음. 실제 로고 사용 금지.

cards.title: A hotel group wants in.
body: The operations manager of a 30-hotel group finds you. Her shift managers want the app for handover notes between day and night teams. Her offer is worth more than ten agency customers combined.

options.text: Take it, and change the homepage to *Notes for every team*
options.feedback: You gain a big customer and lose the clear story that brings agencies in. You'd be back where you started: good, but easy to ignore.

options.text: Take it as a direct deal, but keep your public position on client-service firms
options.feedback: You get the revenue and learn whether hotels could become a future segment, while agencies still see an app built for them. Watch that custom requests don't take over your roadmap.

options.text: Turn it down to stay focused
options.feedback: Your story stays clean, but you give up revenue and a chance to learn. A position limits what you claim in public, not who is allowed to buy.

cards.title: A position is a bet, not a fortress.
body: A narrow position works only if the segment is big enough to grow in. If there turn out to be too few client-service firms, you'll have to widen, and that's harder once people know you as the agency app.
Rivals move too. If a big note app adds one-click summaries, your point of difference shrinks. Then you'll need a new one, or a clear way to show why their version doesn't fit client work.

cards.title: Four decisions, one clear place in the customer's mind.
body: Each decision matches an idea from this unit.
list: **Decision 1 · Frame of reference:** choose what customers compare you with
**Decision 2 · Points of difference:** lead with a reason that matters, that you do better, and that rivals don't claim
**Decision 3 · Owning one word:** one clear idea beats twelve features
**Decision 4 · Positioning basics:** a position decides what you claim, not who may buy
cards.callout: **Try it today:** finish this sentence for your business: "For ___, we're the ___ that ___, unlike ___." If you can't fill a blank, that's your next decision.
